title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
dek: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
why: This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to norms — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.
who: Engineers and founders working on medical AI products, clinical validation or regulatory submissions, and researchers interested in how evidence standards for medical AI get established.
skip: The personal-history parts of the lightning round (first job, favorite paper) can be skipped.

points.h: Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up to scrutiny
points.body: Around 2019, new papers appeared every week claiming "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," yet these conclusions contradicted one another. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something nobody was doing at the time: they took the rigor standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years and applied them to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, head-to-head comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down drastically — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small handful, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there is too much noise in the published literature.

points.h: Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
points.body: CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially a checklist specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they are not methodology guidelines, they are transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs and no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu added a side effect: when authors know they must report a certain item, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that is hard to measure.

points.h: Guidelines come out of Delphi voting; items that can't reach consensus get cut
points.body: CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI were not written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion produced a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, ending with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable part, because people learn from one another. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that reach consensus are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project well takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and getting high-quality feedback and multi-round participation means you can't cut corners on time or reach.

points.h: Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines split the room
points.body: Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was whether clinical trials should include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluations you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said "No, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That debate was later commissioned as a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most-cited papers. In the lightning round, Xiao Liu also clearly took the "no" side: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI to be explainable, and keep asking all the way down — what you ultimately want is just beneficial outcomes.

points.h: Advising regulators without ever working in industry felt insincere to her
points.body: At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulatory agencies. She began to feel she had never stood on the side of the regulated, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product-shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

points.h: Short term, computer scientists set the direction; long term, clinicians gatekeep
points.body: Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first pushed back on what "driven" means, and after confirming it meant "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is that the people handling the data, choosing the metrics and choosing the benchmarks determine in the short term which direction progress moves; but if the endpoint is genuinely being used on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

points.h: Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
points.body: Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the center of gravity shifts to being "a companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, day-to-day wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She thinks people will continuously need something deeply interpersonal on this journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

points.h: The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we won't dare
points.body: Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives the example of inflammatory eye diseases from her doctoral research: a bunch of diseases are loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are very likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way the new intelligence shows up is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: this field is inherently cautious and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, sticking rigidly during a period of new technological change to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, and missing the chance to discover.

terms.def: Multiple rounds of anonymous voting plus an in-person discussion, used to reach consensus among experts on which items matter.
The international checklist of what a randomized controlled trial paper must report; the AI version is CONSORT AI.
The reporting checklist for clinical trial protocol papers; the AI version is SPIRIT AI.
A loose umbrella term for a group of inflammatory eye diseases that produce white dots in the fundus, possibly driven by different mechanisms.
